swap.title: How mem::swap works
swap.description: Exchanges the values of two variables without copying either.

slides.caption: swap takes two mutable references and trades their contents.
The value of a moves to b…
…and the value of b moves to a, at the same time. No clone is made.
Works for any type, even ones that cannot be copied or cloned.

replace.title: How mem::replace works
replace.description: Puts a new value into a place and returns the old one.

slides.caption: You cannot move a value out of a &mut without putting something back. replace does both at once.
The old Vec [1, 2] is moved out and returned.
The new Vec [9] takes its place, so v is never left empty.
Typical inside methods that take &mut self and need to take ownership of a field.

take.title: How mem::take works
take.description: Moves a value out and leaves the type's default (empty) value behind.

slides.caption: take is replace with the default value: an empty Vec, an empty String, 0.
The full Vec is moved out.
An empty Vec is left in its place.
The type must implement Default. For Option, opt.take() does the same and leaves None.

size_of.title: How mem::size_of works
size_of.description: How many bytes a value of a type takes in memory.

slides.caption: The size is fixed per type and known at compile time.
(u8, u32) is 8, not 5: padding keeps the u32 aligned.
A Vec or String is always 24 bytes on 64-bit (pointer, length, capacity), however much it holds.

size_of_val.title: How mem::size_of_val works
size_of_val.description: The size in bytes of the value you point at, even for slices and str.

slides.caption: For a slice the size depends on the length; size_of_val measures the actual value.
For a str, size_of_val equals s.len().

align_of.title: How mem::align_of works
align_of.description: The address multiple a type must be stored at.

slides.caption: A u32 must start at an address divisible by 4; that is why structs get padding.
Only matters for low-level code, FFI and unsafe pointer work.

drop.title: How drop works
drop.description: Destroys a value now, instead of at the end of its scope.

slides.caption: drop takes ownership and lets the value go out of scope at once.
The lock is held by guard.
drop(guard) ends its life right here.
The resource is free before the function ends.
drop is just fn drop<T>(_x: T) {}: moving the value in is what destroys it.

forget.title: How mem::forget works
forget.description: Gives up a value without running its destructor.

slides.caption: forget is safe but leaks: the value's memory and resources are never released.
The value is moved into forget.
Rarely needed outside FFI; prefer ManuallyDrop or Box::leak.

discriminant.title: How mem::discriminant works
discriminant.description: Compares which enum variant two values are, ignoring their data.

slides.caption: The data inside does not matter, only the variant.
Some(1) and Some(99): both Some, true.
matches!(x, Some(_)) is simpler when you know the variant you want.

needs_drop.title: How mem::needs_drop works
needs_drop.description: Whether dropping a type runs any code.

slides.caption: Plain numbers need no clean-up; types that own heap memory do.
String and Vec free their buffers.
Used by collection code to skip loops over items that need no dropping.

new.title: How ManuallyDrop::new works
new.description: Wraps a value so its destructor does not run automatically.

slides.caption: Used in low-level code that controls drop order itself.
Leaving the scope does not drop it.
into_inner gives the value back so it drops normally.

into_inner.title: How ManuallyDrop::into_inner works
into_inner.description: Unwraps the value, so it is dropped normally again.

slides.caption: Written as a function call, not a method, on purpose.
It drops when its scope ends.

maybe_uninit-new.title: How MaybeUninit::new works
maybe_uninit-new.description: A MaybeUninit that is already initialised with a value.

slides.caption: MaybeUninit lets low-level code handle memory that may not be filled yet.

uninit.title: How MaybeUninit::uninit works
uninit.description: Reserves space for a value without initialising it.

slides.caption: Reading before writing would be undefined behaviour.
Box::new_uninit does this on the heap.

write.title: How MaybeUninit::write works
write.description: Stores a value into the slot and returns a &mut to it.

slides.caption: Safe: it never reads the old (garbage) contents.

zeroed.title: How MaybeUninit::zeroed works
zeroed.description: A slot whose memory is filled with zero bytes.

slides.caption: For integers, all-zero is a valid value; for references it is not.
Only assume_init when zero is valid for the type.

align_of_val.title: How mem::align_of_val works
align_of_val.description: The alignment of the value you point at.

slides.caption: For slices it is the alignment of the element type.
align_of::<T>() when you know the type.

assume_init.title: How MaybeUninit::assume_init works
assume_init.description: Declares the slot initialised and takes the value out (unsafe).

slides.caption: Calling it on uninitialised memory is undefined behaviour.

assume_init_read.title: How MaybeUninit::assume_init_read works
assume_init_read.description: Copies the value out while leaving the slot as it is (unsafe).

slides.caption: For non-Copy types, avoid using both copies.

assume_init_ref.title: How MaybeUninit::assume_init_ref works
assume_init_ref.description: A shared reference to the initialised value (unsafe).

assume_init_mut.title: How MaybeUninit::assume_init_mut works
assume_init_mut.description: A mutable reference to the initialised value (unsafe).

assume_init_drop.title: How MaybeUninit::assume_init_drop works
assume_init_drop.description: Drops the value inside the slot in place (unsafe).

slides.caption: Afterwards the slot is uninitialised again.
MaybeUninit never drops its contents by itself.

as_ptr.title: How MaybeUninit::as_ptr works
as_ptr.description: A *const T to the slot's contents.

slides.caption: Reading is only valid once initialised.

as_mut_ptr.title: How MaybeUninit::as_mut_ptr works
as_mut_ptr.description: A *mut T to the slot, for initialising it piece by piece.

slides.caption: Useful for structs filled field by field.
Do not create &mut to uninitialised memory.

assume_init_ref_slice.title: How [MaybeUninit<T>]::assume_init_ref works
assume_init_ref_slice.description: Views a slice of initialised slots as &[T] (unsafe).

assume_init_drop_slice.title: How [MaybeUninit<T>]::assume_init_drop works
assume_init_drop_slice.description: Drops every value in a slice of initialised slots (unsafe).

write_copy_of_slice.title: How [MaybeUninit<T>]::write_copy_of_slice works
write_copy_of_slice.description: Initialises a buffer by copying a slice into it; returns &mut [T].

write_clone_of_slice.title: How [MaybeUninit<T>]::write_clone_of_slice works
write_clone_of_slice.description: Initialises a buffer with clones of a slice's elements.

slides.caption: Remember to drop the contents later.

manually_drop-drop.title: How ManuallyDrop::drop works
manually_drop-drop.description: Runs the wrapped value's destructor now (unsafe).

slides.caption: Do not use the value afterwards.
The wrapper stays but is empty.

manually_drop-take.title: How ManuallyDrop::take works
manually_drop-take.description: Moves the value out of the wrapper, leaving it logically empty (unsafe).

slides.caption: The wrapper must not be used again.
into_inner when you can consume the wrapper.

transmute_copy.title: How mem::transmute_copy works
transmute_copy.description: Reads the bytes of a value as another type (unsafe).

slides.caption: The source may be larger than the target.
f32::to_bits is the safe way here.

mem-zeroed.title: How mem::zeroed works
mem-zeroed.description: A value whose bytes are all zero (unsafe).

slides.caption: Only valid for types where zero is a valid value (not references or NonZero).
Default::default() is the safe way for most types.
